slides.title: Why automated testing matters for AI-generated code
bullets: AI code is nondeterministic and may hide subtle bugs
Manual review does not scale with generated volume
Automated pipelines give fast, repeatable confidence
Testing must cover syntax, semantics, and runtime behavior
slides.notes: AI-native software factories produce large amounts of code from models that can hallucinate or misinterpret specifications. Because the output varies across runs, a single manual inspection cannot guarantee quality. Automated testing provides a systematic, repeatable way to catch regressions, enforce contracts, and measure reliability before deployment. This slide sets the motivation for the entire lecture.

slides.title: Testing pyramid adapted for AI-native pipelines
bullets: Unit tests: check individual generated functions
Integration tests: verify component interactions
System tests: run end‑to‑end scenarios with real data
Property‑based tests: express invariants that must hold for all outputs
slides.notes: The classic testing pyramid still applies, but the layers shift. Unit tests are often generated alongside code; integration tests must exercise the boundaries where AI‑generated modules meet hand‑written ones; system tests use realistic workloads; property‑based tests capture high‑level specifications that are hard to enumerate as concrete cases. This structure guides where to invest automation effort.

slides.title: Static analysis and specification‑driven checks
bullets: Specifications written in a formal or semi‑formal language
A spec checker verifies generated code against the spec
Catches type errors, contract violations, and missing cases
Runs before any code execution, cheap and fast
slides.notes: Specification‑driven development (C2) lets developers write pre‑ and post‑conditions, invariants, or interface contracts. A static verifier then proves that the generated implementation satisfies those contracts without executing it. This early gate eliminates a whole class of defects and reduces the load on later dynamic testing stages.

slides.title: Specification‑driven example (pseudocode)
bullets: Spec: sort(input) returns output such that output is a permutation of input and is sorted
Generated code: function sort(arr) { … }
Static checker validates: isPermutation(input, output) ∧ isSorted(output)
Checker runs as a separate tool, not as part of the language runtime

figure.caption: Pseudocode illustration of a spec and a static check

slides.notes: The slide shows a tiny contract for a sorting function. The spec states two post‑conditions: the output must be a permutation of the input and must be sorted. The generated code is not executed; instead a separate verification tool (e.g., an SMT‑based checker) proves that the implementation meets the spec for all possible inputs. This illustrates how static specification checks differ from ordinary type checking.

slides.title: Dynamic testing: execution‑based test generation
bullets: Fuzzing generated functions with random inputs
Property‑based frameworks (e.g., Hypothesis) derive test cases from specs
Differential testing: compare AI output with a trusted reference
Collect coverage to guide further generation
slides.notes: Static checks cannot catch all semantic errors. Dynamic testing runs the code. Fuzzing explores the input space automatically; property‑based testing turns specifications into executable predicates; differential testing uses a known‑good implementation as an oracle. Coverage feedback can be fed back to the model to improve future generations (see C3 on complexity backpressure).

slides.title: Mutation testing for AI‑generated code
bullets: Inject small syntactic changes into generated code
Run test suite; surviving mutants indicate weak tests
Helps measure test adequacy beyond coverage
Can be automated in CI pipelines
slides.notes: Mutation testing evaluates the quality of the test suite itself. By systematically mutating the generated code (e.g., flipping operators, changing constants) and checking whether tests fail, we learn whether the tests would catch real defects. This is especially valuable for AI code where the test suite may also be generated.

slides.title: Learned evaluators: LLM‑as‑judge and reward models
bullets: LLM‑as‑judge: a separate model scores candidate outputs
Reward models predict human preference or quality signals
They estimate style, readability, or adherence to instructions
Functional correctness still requires execution‑based tests
slides.notes: Learned evaluators are useful for ranking many candidates quickly. A reward model is trained on human feedback and predicts which output a person would prefer. However, it does not execute code, so it cannot reliably certify functional correctness. Execution‑based tests remain the ground truth for correctness; reward models complement them by filtering obvious low‑quality samples.

slides.title: Evaluation metrics for code generation
bullets: Pass@k: probability that at least one of k samples passes hidden tests
Syntax correctness: fraction of parsable programs
Semantic similarity: e.g., CodeBLEU, execution match
Runtime performance: latency, memory within limits
slides.notes: Pass@k is the standard metric in code generation benchmarks (C1). It is defined as the probability that at least one of k independently sampled candidates passes the hidden test suite. The unbiased estimator counts, for each problem, how many of the k samples pass and applies the formula 1 - C(n‑c, k) / C(n, k) where n is total samples and c is passing samples. Syntax and semantic metrics give complementary views.

slides.title: Computing Pass@k from sample results (illustrative)
bullets: Problem: 100 samples generated, 30 pass hidden tests
Numbers are illustrative; real benchmarks use many problems
slides.notes: This table walks through the unbiased estimator for Pass@k. With 100 generated samples and 30 that pass, the chance that a random set of 10 contains at least one passing sample is about 96%. The calculation uses combinatorics; in practice libraries compute it directly. The figures are purely illustrative to show the mechanics.

slides.title: Benchmark suites for code generation
bullets: HumanEval: 164 Python problems with unit tests
MBPP: 974 basic programming problems
APPS: 10,000 problems from easy to competition level
Benchmarks enable reproducible comparison of models and pipelines
slides.notes: Standard benchmarks provide a common ground for evaluating code generation. HumanEval and MBPP focus on functional correctness; APPS adds algorithmic difficulty. When reporting Pass@k or other metrics, always state the benchmark and the exact evaluation protocol (temperature, number of samples, test suite version).

slides.title: Reliability requirements and test adequacy criteria
bullets: Safety‑critical: require mutation score > 90% and zero critical mutants
Business‑critical: target Pass@k ≥ 0.95 on representative benchmarks
Regulatory: traceability from requirement to test case
Adequacy criteria guide where to invest testing effort
slides.notes: Different domains impose different reliability targets. Safety‑critical systems often mandate high mutation scores and evidence that all requirements are exercised. Business‑critical AI services may set a Pass@k threshold on a curated benchmark. Explicit adequacy criteria turn vague quality goals into measurable testing objectives.

Pipeline B: LLM‑as‑judge filter + lightweight unit tests

Assumed false‑negative rate: A low, B moderate (illustrative)
Measurement method: run both pipelines on a fixed benchmark set, record cost, latency, and defect escape rate

The rightmost column describes how each criterion would be measured in practice: instrument the CI system for cost, seed known mutants for false‑negative rate, timestamp pipeline stages for latency, and monitor production for escaped defects. slides.title: Check: Pass@k definition

quiz.question: What does Pass@k measure in code generation evaluation?
options: The fraction of generated programs that compile successfully
The probability that at least one of k sampled candidates passes the hidden tests
The average similarity score between generated and reference solutions
The percentage of test cases covered by the generated code
quiz.explanation: Pass@k is defined as the probability that at least one of k independently sampled candidates passes the hidden test suite. Option 0 describes syntax correctness, option 2 describes semantic similarity metrics like CodeBLEU, and option 3 describes test coverage. The most tempting wrong answer is option 0 because compilation is a prerequisite but not the definition of Pass@k.

slides.notes: This question checks the precise definition of Pass@k, a core metric for the learning outcome. The explanation clarifies why the other options are related but distinct concepts.

slides.title: Check: Role of reward models

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the role of a reward model in AI code generation pipelines?
options: It executes generated code and reports pass/fail results
It predicts human preference or quality signals without running the code
It formally verifies that the code satisfies a given specification
It mutates the code to assess test suite adequacy
quiz.explanation: Reward models are trained on human feedback to predict which outputs humans would prefer; they do not execute code, perform formal verification, or conduct mutation testing. Option 0 describes execution‑based testing, option 2 describes static specification checking, and option 3 describes mutation testing. The most tempting wrong answer is option 0 because both reward models and execution tests are used for quality assessment, but they operate differently.

slides.notes: This question reinforces the distinction between learned evaluators and execution‑based correctness checks, a key point for comparing testing mechanisms.

slides.title: Summary: Automated testing and evaluation mechanisms
bullets: Static spec checks catch contract violations early
Dynamic testing (fuzzing, property‑based, differential) validates runtime behavior
Mutation testing measures test suite quality
Learned evaluators rank candidates but cannot replace execution tests
Pass@k and benchmark suites provide standardized effectiveness metrics
Reliability requirements drive adequacy criteria and pipeline design
slides.notes: Recap the main mechanisms: static specification‑driven verification, dynamic execution‑based testing, mutation analysis, learned evaluators, and quantitative metrics. Emphasize that each mechanism addresses different reliability requirements and that a robust AI‑native pipeline combines them in a layered fashion. This summary directly supports CO4.LO1.
